components.title: Accordion
components.summary: Groups related content under a heading that users expand or collapse; the heading names the hidden content.

whenToUse: When a page covers many topics and needs clear structure, when space is tight, especially on mobile, or when users should choose which content to read.
dos: Give each accordion a clear, precise heading that describes the information it contains.
donts: Do not nest accordions for complex content; it confuses users and makes navigation harder.

docs.summary: Accordion groups information under headings and lets users show or hide the related content. The page explains when accordions help - structure on content-heavy pages, saving space on mobile and giving users control - the heading and icon that signal state, the print caveat and layout advice such as 60-90 characters per line.

sections.heading: Kurzbeschreibung
sections.summary: An accordion groups information under headings and lets users expand or collapse the related content.

sections.heading: Beschreibung
sections.summary: Clicking or tapping the heading shows or hides the content beneath it. The title summarises what is inside, and an icon indicates whether the section is expanded or collapsed.

sections.heading: Verwendungsregeln
sections.summary: Accordions structure pages with many topics, save space on mobile and give users control over what they read. Expanding pushes content down, which can disorient; printing is often poor, so offer an expand-all control or expand on print.

sections.heading: Dos und Don’ts
sections.summary: Give every accordion a clear, precise heading that describes the information it contains. Do not nest accordions for complex content - it confuses users and makes navigation harder.

sections.heading: Weitere Hinweise
sections.summary: Use accordions to compress content on mobile. Keep them 60-90 characters wide and consistent, avoid auto-collapsing, and skip them on sparse pages or where uninterrupted reading is needed.

components.title: Alert
components.summary: Shows a short, colour-coded notice about important information, with optional description and link.

whenToUse: When important information or a change must reach the user and a short notice with an optional link is enough.
dos: Use alerts sparingly; information can also be conveyed in a paragraph of text.
Describe the reason for the alert in a brief and precise explanation.
If user action is required, name and/or link that action.
donts: Do not leave users alone with a message; point out solutions.

docs.summary: Alert flags important information or a change with a short notice. It has a header with an icon and descriptive title, an optional body text and an optional link, and four fixed colour-coded tones: info (blue), success (green), warning (yellow) and danger (red). The page explains effective use, the meaning of each tone and when not to use an alert.

sections.heading: Kurzbeschreibung
sections.summary: An alert flags important information with a short explanation and an optional link.

sections.heading: Beschreibung
sections.summary: An alert has a header of icon plus descriptive title and an optional content area with a short text and an optional link to more information or related actions. Four fixed tones: info (blue), success (green), warning (yellow), danger (red).

sections.heading: Effektiver Einsatz
sections.summary: Keep the message clear and unambiguous, show alerts only when they are relevant for the user, communicate urgency appropriately, and let users react to the message directly.

sections.heading: Verwendungsregeln
sections.summary: Info (blue) for uncritical status without action; success (green) for a completed action; warning (yellow) for attention without criticality, stating whether an action is required; danger (red) for a critical state that blocks progress, naming or linking the needed action.

sections.heading: Dos und Don’ts
sections.summary: Use alerts sparingly - a plain text paragraph can carry the information. Describe the reason briefly and precisely, name or link any required user action, and never leave users alone with a message without solutions.

components.title: Badge
components.summary: Compact, non-interactive status hint on a parent element: an icon plus a short label in one of four tones.

whenToUse: When the status of an element must be shown compactly at a glance, especially in overviews and lists.
dos: Make sure badges do not cover other elements.
When space is tight, reduce the badge to its label or icon if the meaning survives.
donts: Do not change the badge colour scheme.
Do not give one object several statuses.
Do not use badges for complex status information; use Alert, Notification or Toast instead.

docs.summary: Badge gives a very short status hint on a parent element, built from an icon and a short label. The page covers the 8px grid sizing, the four fixed tones and their uses, how the icon is hidden from or exposed to screen readers, the layout rules, and how to shrink a badge when space is tight.

sections.heading: Kurzbeschreibung
sections.summary: A badge gives a short status hint about a parent element.

sections.heading: Badge-Dimensionen
sections.summary: Badge scaling follows the system-wide 8px grid.

sections.heading: Beschreibung
sections.summary: A badge is a compact, non-interactive status hint on a parent element, e.g. whether a request was transmitted, is in progress or hit a problem. It pairs an icon with a short, precise label; drop the icon when space is tight if the meaning survives. Use Alert for immediate feedback on an action.

sections.heading: Verwendungsregeln
sections.summary: Badges give a very short status for orientation, mainly in overviews, and signal whether the user must act. Info: stable, no action. Success: done or ready. Warning: open, needs attention or action. Danger: user action required, so link to detail.

sections.heading: Badge mit Icon
sections.summary: The component sets aria-hidden="true" on the icon by default, because the label usually carries the meaning. To expose the icon to screen readers, set aria-hidden to false and add an aria-label.

sections.heading: Dos und Don’ts
sections.summary: Make sure badges do not cover other elements, do not change the colour scheme, and do not give one object several statuses.

sections.heading: Weitere Hinweise
sections.summary: When space is tight, reduce the badge to its label or icon if the meaning survives. More complex status messages are better communicated with Alert, Notification or Toast.

components.title: Bildwortmarke
components.summary: Official umbrella mark that identifies Bund, Länder and Kommunen offers; supplied as protected graphics, not as code.

dos: Follow the style guide and the terms of use.
Use the mark only as a public body, to identify Bund, Länder and Kommunen offers.
Keep the clear space around the mark free of other elements.
Use the image alone without the wordmark only in compact formats such as favicons or app icons.
donts: Do not change the mark's size, colour, typeface or wordmark position.
Do not distort, squash, crop, alter, flip or rotate the mark.
Do not place the mark on coloured backgrounds or images without the white carrier surface.

docs.summary: The Bildwortmarke is the umbrella mark that identifies cross-level services of Bund, Länder and Kommunen. The page describes it - a federal eagle image plus the wordmark "Bund Länder Kommunen" - where it may be placed, the mandatory clear space, the Do's and Don'ts, and how to obtain the graphics and style guide, which KERN supplies separately and without EUPL licence.

sections.heading: Kurzbeschreibung
sections.summary: The Bildwortmarke marks administrative services of Bund, Länder and Kommunen and works as a recognisable sender mark, like a quality seal.

sections.heading: Beschreibung
sections.summary: A modern interpretation of the federal eagle in the national colours black, red and gold, built from 16 elements, with the wordmark "Bund Länder Kommunen" to its right in a fixed typeface. A lightened colour variant exists for dark themes.

sections.heading: Verwendungsregeln
sections.summary: Voluntary mark that supplements, never replaces, Länder and Kommunen marks; only one sender per header. Place it top left for cross-level offers, or in the footer with the prescribed descriptor. Keep its clear space empty; custom wordmarks go through beantragen@dachmarke.gov.de.

sections.heading: Do's
sections.summary: Follow the style guide and terms of use. Only public bodies may use the mark. Keep the clear space free. Use the image alone without the wordmark only in compact formats such as favicons or app icons.

sections.heading: Don'ts
sections.summary: Do not change size, colour, typeface or wordmark position; do not distort, squash, crop, alter, flip or rotate it; do not place it on coloured backgrounds or images without the white carrier surface.

sections.heading: Bereitstellung
sections.summary: It is an official state mark, so KERN provides neither EUPL licence nor source code. Graphics and the full style guide come as a password-protected ZIP; request the password and usage rights from beantragen@dachmarke.gov.de.

components.title: Body
components.summary: Running-text component in three sizes with bold and muted styles; the base for longer readable content.

whenToUse: When longer information should be presented as readable running text.
dos: Use Body only for running text; use Link or Heading for content that has its own component.
Use the given sizes and styles instead of manual bold or font-size changes.
Use body--small and body--large sparingly, and body--muted only in exceptions.
donts: Do not embed text as an image unless it can be fully adjusted, e.g. font size, colour and background.

docs.summary: Body is the running-text component for longer information. The page defines its three sizes (small, default, large) plus the bold and muted styles, when large fits an entry page, small suits supplementary text or dense tables, and muted is only for marginal notes, and the rule never to fake formatting by hand.

sections.heading: Kurzbeschreibung
sections.summary: Body conveys longer information in written form.

sections.heading: Beschreibung
sections.summary: Body is a text component for running text in three sizes - small, default and large. It is the textual base for longer content and is designed for good readability.

sections.heading: Verwendungsregeln
sections.summary: Use Body for running text that conveys facts. body--large: one intro paragraph per page on entry or landing pages. body--small: short supplementary text or dense tables, not key information. body--bold emphasises phrases; use inline links in text. body--muted: marginal notes or legal footnotes only.

sections.heading: Dos und Don’ts
sections.summary: Use Body only for running text, not for content that has its own component such as Link or Heading. Never fake formatting by hand - use the given sizes and styles. Use small and large sparingly and muted only in exceptions.

sections.heading: Weitere Hinweise
sections.summary: Check whether extensive content is better split across several pages or sections.

components.title: Button
components.summary: Triggers an action, named by its label, in primary, secondary or tertiary importance; one primary per page.

whenToUse: When the user triggers an action such as confirming, submitting, changing data or moving to the next step.
dos: Use only one primary button per page.
Use mixed case labels rather than all capitals.
When buttons of different importance sit together, highlight the more important one.
Place buttons side by side rather than stacked when space allows.
donts: Avoid two-line or multi-line button labels.
Do not use buttons inline in texts; use text links instead.
Avoid inactive buttons where possible; their contrast is poor and they are easily confused with other buttons.

docs.summary: Button triggers an action and its label names it. The page sets the 48 px default size and 8 px scale, describes the five sizes and the larger functional hit area of x-small and small, the primary, secondary and tertiary importance levels, icon use, when to avoid inactive buttons, the mobile block button, and label and placement rules.

sections.heading: Kurzbeschreibung
sections.summary: A button triggers an action; its label names that action.

sections.heading: Button-Dimensionen
sections.summary: The button system uses a 48 px default size; the other sizes scale in consistent 8 px steps.

sections.heading: Größenübersicht
sections.summary: Sizes refer to the visual height. On x-small and small the functional click area extends beyond the visible surface, so the target stays large enough in compact or dense layouts.

sections.heading: Beschreibung
sections.summary: A button lets users trigger an action, such as confirming, submitting information, changing data or moving to the next process step. It carries a label describing the action briefly and precisely, and may include icons for visual support.

sections.heading: Verwendungsregeln
sections.summary: Three levels: primary triggers the page's main function and appears once per page; secondary supports it, e.g. cancel or back, and should stay rare; tertiary marks functions unrelated to the main one, such as sorting, while still reading as a control.

sections.heading: Icons
sections.summary: Add icons only when they speed up understanding, e.g. a left arrow to go back, a bin to delete, a magnifier to search. The icon sits before the label by default, after it when that aids comprehension. Icon-only buttons need a familiar icon and an alt attribute.

sections.heading: Inaktiv
sections.summary: Inactive buttons show that a function exists but is unavailable. Because of poor contrast and confusion with other buttons, avoid them if possible; use them only when they aid understanding, recognition or consistency.

sections.heading: Block-Button
sections.summary: Use the block button in mobile views: its width follows the screen rather than the text length, which makes the layout clearer.

sections.heading: Dos und Don’ts
sections.summary: Use one primary button per page, mixed case instead of capitals, and place buttons side by side rather than stacked when there is room, highlighting the more important one. Avoid two-line labels and never put buttons inline in text; use text links.

components.title: Card
components.summary: Presents one related content unit in a distinct area with Media, Header, Body and Footer regions.

whenToUse: When related content such as image, text and actions should be shown compactly in one separated area.
dos: Give each card one clear focus and only one connected information unit or task.
Keep all cards in a context at the same size, structure and spacing.
donts: Do not use cards for long texts or complex tables.
Do not use different card sizes in the same context.
Do not overload the card with too many actions or buttons.
Do not use redundant information across several cards.
Do not use more than one media item in a card.

docs.summary: Card presents related content compactly in a visually separated area built from Media, Header, Body and Footer. The page covers what each region holds, the three sizes and the fully interactive variant, grid placement, and rules for a clear focus, consistent sizing, reduced content and sparing use of actions.

sections.heading: Kurzbeschreibung
sections.summary: Presents compact, related content in a visually separated area.

sections.heading: Beschreibung
sections.summary: A card presents one content unit in a distinct area with four regions: Media holds the image, Header can add Preline and Subline, Body takes your own or KERN components such as Description List, and Footer holds one or two buttons. Cards fit a grid, may be fully interactive, and come in three sizes.

sections.heading: Verwendungsregeln
sections.summary: Use cards to structure content semantically. Give each card one clear focus and a single information or task unit, using visual hierarchy. Keep cards in one context at the same size, structure and spacing, including media, avoid overload and use interactive elements sparingly.

sections.heading: Dos and Don’ts
sections.summary: Do not use cards for long texts or complex tables. Do not mix card sizes in one context or overload a card with actions. Avoid redundant content across cards, and use at most one media item per card.

components.title: Input Checkboxes
components.summary: Lets users select one or more independent options; use Radios when only one option may be chosen.

whenToUse: For binary decisions such as accepting terms, or for lists in which several options may be selected independently.
dos: Write the checkbox label as a statement rather than a question.
Prefer positive wording and avoid negations in labels.
Keep the label short enough to fit on one line.
donts: Do not use so many checkboxes that the interface becomes cluttered and unclear.
Do not use checkboxes when only one option may be chosen; use Radios instead.

docs.summary: Checkbox lets users select one or more options independently. The page covers labelling each box, the group legend and optional hint, group-level error display, the states shared with Input except readonly, single use for binary decisions and list use, and switching to Radios when only one option may be chosen.

sections.heading: Kurzbeschreibung
sections.summary: A checkbox selects one or more options.

sections.heading: Beschreibung
sections.summary: A checkbox decides whether an option applies; several can be selected independently. Each has a short label; a check mark shows selection. A group needs an unambiguous legend, optionally marked "optional", and may have a hint. Group errors show below; all Input states apply except readonly.

sections.heading: Verwendungsregeln
sections.summary: Use a single checkbox for binary decisions such as accepting privacy terms, or several for selection lists. Add a clear legend when the group's purpose is not clear from the preceding text. The selection is saved only on a confirming button. To allow just one option, use Radios.

sections.heading: Dos und Don’ts
sections.summary: Write labels as statements rather than questions, prefer positive wording without negations, and keep labels short enough to fit one line. Use a checkbox for simple decisions; a Select may fit complex choices. Avoid too many checkboxes.

components.title: Description List
components.summary: Pairs short terms with their descriptions in a row or column layout for a clear information hierarchy.

whenToUse: When terms and definitions need a clear, accessible information hierarchy.
When all terms and definitions should be visible at a glance, e.g. summaries of form entries, specifications or glossaries.
donts: Do not use a Description List for pure enumerations.
Do not overload terms and descriptions with too much content.

docs.summary: Description List pairs terms with their descriptions to give a clear, accessible information hierarchy, for example for form entries, technical specifications or glossaries. The page covers the row and column layouts and their responsive behaviour, when to use Accordion instead, and guidance on term length and list width.

sections.heading: Kurzbeschreibung
sections.summary: Structures the presentation of terms and their definitions.

sections.heading: Beschreibung
sections.summary: A Description List has a term and its description, giving a good overview and a clear, accessible information hierarchy. It suits summarising form entries, technical specifications or glossaries. On wide screens the term can sit left of or above the description; on mobile it always sits above.

sections.heading: Verwendungsregeln
sections.summary: With much content, terms and definitions can be stacked directly. Use the list when everything should be visible at once; otherwise use Accordion. Keep terms short and precise, choose the vertical variant for mostly long terms, and do not make the list too wide.

sections.heading: Dos und Don’ts
sections.summary: Do not use a Description List for pure enumerations, and do not overload terms and descriptions with too much content.

components.title: Details
components.summary: Reveals one region of supplementary information on demand; use Accordion for several independent regions.

whenToUse: For supplementary content relevant to only some users, such as help texts, background, legal notes or definitions.
dos: Use Details only for supplementary information that is not required to understand or finish a task.
Label the control briefly, understandably and unambiguously.
Place Details next to the content it relates to.
Use Accordion when several related information regions should be expanded independently.
donts: Do not hide important notes, error messages or mandatory information inside Details.
Do not use general labels such as "More" or "Details" when they do not say what information appears.
Do not place essential input elements or primary actions only inside Details.

docs.summary: Details reveals supplementary information that only some users need. The page covers the always-visible control and the collapsible region, suitable content such as explanations, help texts, background and legal notes, the rule to use it only when information is not required for the task, and where Accordion fits instead.

sections.heading: Kurzbeschreibung
sections.summary: Reveals supplementary information that is relevant only to part of the users.

sections.heading: Beschreibung
sections.summary: The component has a visible control for opening and closing and a collapsible content area. The control stays visible and describes the content; the expanded area can hold text, lists, links or further content.

sections.heading: Verwendungsregeln
sections.summary: Show supplementary information only on demand: additional explanations, help texts, background information, legal notes or definitions. Reserve it for content relevant to only some users and not needed to understand or finish the task, and keep the summary short, clear and unambiguous.

sections.heading: Dos und Don’ts
sections.summary: Use Details only for supplementary information not needed to understand or complete a task. Label the control briefly and clearly, next to the content it relates to. One region per Details; use Accordion for several. Never hide important notes, error messages or mandatory information.

components.htmlCanonical:
Details zu Punkt XY

Das ist ein Beispiel für die Nutzung von <details> und <summary> für die progressive Offenlegung von Inhalten im Textfluss. Es ist eine native HTML-Lösung, die ohne JavaScript auskommt und von aktuellen Browsern und Screenreadern nativ unterstützt wird. Der eingeblendete Inhalt schiebt nachfolgende Elemente auf der Seite nach unten (Layout-Shift).

components.title: Dialog
components.summary: Modal or non-modal overlay that delivers information and asks for input, confirmation or a decision.

whenToUse: Only when immediate decisions or input are needed, and only for important, time-critical or irreversible actions.
dos: Use non-modal dialogs for supporting information that does not disturb the workflow.
Make sure users can always perform a deliberate action to close the dialog.
Communicate the dialog's purpose with clear headings and specific button labels such as "Speichern" or "Abbrechen".
Make confirmation, input and danger dialogs modal; information dialogs can be non-modal.
donts: Do not use sticky elements such as headers or footers; they overlap content when zoomed.
Do not let a dialog's content grow long; scrolling should be the exception.
Do not close a critical dialog on an overlay click.

docs.summary: Dialog communicates with users, delivers important information and asks for input, confirmation or a decision. The page covers modal and non-modal behaviour, the title, description and button rules, when dialogs are justified, the four use cases, and the JavaScript, form and autofocus implementation details.

sections.heading: Kurzbeschreibung
sections.summary: A dialog communicates with users, conveys important information and asks for input, confirmation or a decision through interaction.

sections.heading: Beschreibung
sections.summary: A dialog appears, overlays the main content and requires deliberate action. It is modal (focus trapped) or non-modal, with title and description. Offer a primary and a secondary button; one secondary suffices to confirm, and a third tertiary button stays exceptional. An "X" closes it.

sections.heading: Verwendungsregeln
sections.summary: Use a dialog only for immediate decisions or input, and sparingly - prefer inline components or tooltips. Keep title and content short; long forms belong on separate pages. Always offer a deliberate close via "X" or Escape; critical dialogs must not close on overlay click.

sections.heading: Dos und Don’ts
sections.summary: Use non-modal dialogs for supporting information that does not disturb the workflow, ensure users can always deliberately close the dialog, and state its purpose with clear headings and specific button labels such as "Speichern" or "Abbrechen". Avoid sticky elements and keep content short.

sections.heading: Dialog mit Javascript öffnen
sections.summary: A dialog can be opened by a button, using data attributes (data-dialog-target) to link buttons to their dialogs.

sections.heading: HMTL
sections.summary: HTML example markup for opening a dialog.

sections.heading: JavaScript
sections.summary: JavaScript example that connects data-dialog-target buttons to showModal(), closes the dialog on background clicks and handles a submit button.

sections.heading: Verhalten
sections.summary: The button carrying data-dialog-target opens its dialog. The dialog closes through the close button or a click on the background.

sections.heading: 1. Einsatz des <form>-Elements im Dialog
sections.summary: The form element structures dialog interactions and enables native browser behaviour such as closing through buttons with formmethod="dialog", and simplifies confirmation or cancel actions.

sections.heading: 2. Verwendung des autofocus-Attributs
sections.summary: autofocus focuses a specific input or button automatically when the dialog opens, improving usability - for example placing the cursor in a field or highlighting the primary button - without extra JavaScript.

sections.heading: 3. Browser-Unterstützung
sections.summary: Modern browsers support the dialog element, formmethod="dialog" and autofocus; consider a polyfill for older browsers and check MDN for compatibility.

components.title: Divider
components.summary: Horizontal line that separates or groups content blocks; use sparingly and only in the prescribed colour.

whenToUse: To separate larger sections of independent content or to structure elements that free space cannot group.
dos: Use the space tokens for the gaps above and below a divider.
donts: Do not use a divider in any colour other than the prescribed one.
Do not use too many dividers; too many lines make an application look unclear.

docs.summary: Divider is a simple horizontal line that separates content blocks into groups and can build hierarchy. The page covers full-width and narrower use, use inside other components with the space tokens, the fixed colour rule, and when free space works better and dividers should stay sparse.

sections.heading: Kurzbeschreibung
sections.summary: A divider visually separates content blocks into groups and can build hierarchy.

sections.heading: Beschreibung
sections.summary: A divider is a simple horizontal line. It can span the full page width or visually separate narrower content blocks, and can create hierarchy to show nested relationships.

sections.heading: Verwendungsregeln
sections.summary: Dividers separate larger sections with independent content and support the information hierarchy of the page. They can also be used inside other components; use the space tokens for the gaps above and below.

sections.heading: Dos und Don’ts
sections.summary: Use dividers only in the prescribed colour.

sections.heading: Weitere Hinweise
sections.summary: Use dividers to structure elements when free space cannot group them, but use them sparingly - too many lines make an application look unclear.

components.title: Dropdown
components.summary: Collapsible menu that bundles actions or links for a parent element.

docs.summary: Dropdown bundles actions or links in a menu that expands from a trigger, so secondary actions do not clutter the main flow.

components.title: Fieldset
components.summary: Groups related form fields with a legend and shared hint or error; required for checkbox and radio groups.

whenToUse: For multi-part entries such as addresses or date fields, and for checkbox or radio groups that relate to one question.
dos: Use fieldsets only for elements that belong together in content.
Use a Fieldset for checkbox lists and radio groups; it is mandatory there.
Give the legend a clear and concise label and never leave it empty.
Link group-level error messages inside the fieldset via aria-describedby.
donts: Do not use a Fieldset for a single checkbox, e.g. accepting a privacy policy.
Do not nest form field groups inside one another.

docs.summary: Fieldset groups related form fields and can build hierarchy, using a legend plus a group of elements. The page covers the kern-label classes and kern-label--large, hint text above and group errors below, vertical or horizontal arrangement via .kern-fieldset__body--horizontal, and when a Fieldset is required.

sections.heading: Kurzbeschreibung
sections.summary: A fieldset groups related form fields visually and semantically and can build hierarchy.

sections.heading: Beschreibung
sections.summary: A fieldset pairs a legend with a group of related form elements. The legend names the group concisely and aids orientation, especially for assistive technology; it uses kern-label, enlargeable with kern-label--large. Hints sit above the group, group errors below, and elements can be horizontal.

sections.heading: Verwendungsregeln
sections.summary: Group related form elements logically, whatever the input type, to improve structure and screen-reader support. It suits multi-part entries such as addresses or dates, and checkbox or radio groups answering one question. Group errors belong inside the fieldset, linked via aria-describedby.

sections.heading: Dos und Don’ts
sections.summary: Use fieldsets only for related elements; they are mandatory for checkbox lists and radios, but not for a single checkbox such as a privacy consent. Use one only when a shared legend, error and hint make sense, label the legend clearly, never leave it empty, and never nest field groups.

docs.summary: Low-level access to CSS Grid for complex layouts without custom CSS. A wrapper .kern-grid defines the grid with display: grid and replaces the classic .kern-row architecture; columns and gaps are set through modifier classes.

sections.heading: Beschreibung
sections.summary: Grid display classes: .kern-grid (display: grid, default 12 columns and gap-lg) and .kern-inline-grid. Column and row counts come from .kern-grid-cols-{n} (1-12) and .kern-grid-rows-{n} (1-6); gaps from .kern-gap-{size}[-{breakpoint}], also .kern-gap-x-{size} and .kern-gap-y-{size}.

sections.heading: Spalten-Platzierung (Items)
sections.summary: Places items in the grid: .kern-col-{n}[-{breakpoint}] spans n columns, .kern-col-start-{n} and .kern-col-end-{n} set the start or end column line.

sections.heading: Drei Spalten Layout
sections.summary: Example that creates three equally wide columns across all viewports.

sections.heading: Responsive Anpassung
sections.summary: Responsive suffixes adapt the layout; the example starts with 2 columns on mobile and switches to 4 columns from the md breakpoint.

sections.heading: 1. Raster Definition
sections.summary: Defines the basic grid structure on the container.

sections.heading: 2. Abstände (Gap)
sections.summary: Controls the gap between columns and rows.

sections.heading: 3. Wrapping
sections.summary: Grid items wrap automatically onto the next row once more than the available 12 columns are occupied.

sections.heading: 4. Positionierung (Starts & Ends)
sections.summary: Replaces traditional offsets: it states explicitly where an element starts or ends.

sections.heading: 5. Automatische Spalten (Auto Columns)
sections.summary: Items without an explicit column class occupy one unit of the 12-column grid by default. .kern-col-auto sizes an item from its content but keeps it inside the grid: in CSS Grid it takes exactly one grid cell regardless of content width.

sections.heading: 6. Verschachtelung (Nesting)
sections.summary: Grids can be nested without limit. The inner grid does not inherit the parent's column count; it defines a new grid context.

sections.heading: Breakpoints
sections.summary: All classes follow the mobile-first approach.

sections.heading: Dos and Don'ts
sections.summary: Do use kern-gap to define spacing, and kern-col-full for elements that should break out of the grid. Do not mix kern-row (legacy) with kern-grid syntax.

components.title: Header
components.summary: Header carries a page's central navigation: logo, main menu and key actions.

docs.summary: Header provides a page's central navigation: the logo, the main menu and the most important actions, so key areas are reachable from the top of the page.

components.title: Heading
components.summary: Headings label and structure a page and its sections; mark them up with h1-h6 and keep the outline in order.

whenToUse: Use headings for the page title and for every section, so the page stays scannable for people and machines.
Choose the visual size from the depth of the outline on the page.
dos: Mark every heading with the matching HTML tag such as h1 or h2.
Keep exactly one h1 per page.
Keep the hierarchy in order: never place an h3 or h4 before an h2.
Write headings in regular sentence case, not in capitals.
Keep headings short and free of manual line breaks.
Add the matching CSS class so headings stay visually consistent.
donts: Don't build headings with manual bold or font-size formatting; search engines and screen readers will not recognise them.
Don't use Heading Display to structure content; it is only for standout statements.

docs.summary: Headings label and structure a page and its sections. Mark each one with the matching HTML heading tag so browsers, search engines and assistive technology read the outline correctly, and add the KERN class for consistent styling. One h1 per page, a strict hierarchy underneath, short sentence-case wording.

sections.heading: Kurzbeschreibung
sections.summary: A Heading structures and describes content sections so that users and assistive technology can orient themselves quickly.

sections.heading: Beschreibung
sections.summary: Headings divide a page into clear sections and summarise the text below them. They are part of the semantic document structure, so correct markup is what lets content be captured, found and read accessibly.

sections.heading: Verwendungsregeln
sections.summary: Always mark headings with the proper HTML tag such as h1 or h2 to keep the page's semantic structure, and add a matching CSS class so they stay visually consistent. Use headings for the page and for every section.

sections.heading: Übersicht: Rolle und Verwendung von Überschriftenelementen
sections.summary: Explains the role of each element: the title tag sets the browser tab and search result title, h1 is the one visible main heading per page, h2 marks each top-level section, and h3 and h4 divide an h2 section further.

sections.heading: Anwendung der visuellen und semantischen Hierarchie
sections.summary: Pick the visual size from the number of hierarchy levels on the page, so the outline stays clear even on more complex pages.

sections.heading: Seiten mit vier und mehr Ebenen
sections.summary: On pages with four or more levels the usual visual hierarchy may be departed from in special cases, such as the Alert component. Make sure the page stays accessible, especially for screen reader users.

sections.heading: Display-Überschrift
sections.summary: Heading Display is a very large heading for standout statements, not for structuring content. Use it only in exceptions, for example a landing page opening line, a personal greeting or the framing of a special area. Mark it up semantically and check how it renders on small devices.

sections.heading: Dos und Don’ts
sections.summary: One h1 per page, never fake a heading with bold text or font sizes because search engines and screen readers will not recognise it, no h3 or h4 before an h2, and write headings in regular sentence case rather than capitals.

sections.heading: Weitere Hinweise
sections.summary: Keep headings short, use them to structure the content, consider splitting very long pages into several, and avoid manually inserted line breaks inside a heading.

components.title: Icon
components.summary: Icons are small Material Symbols that mark actions, content or status, used sparingly with one meaning per icon.

whenToUse: Use an icon only where it adds value, for example to mark an action or a status.
dos: Use Material Symbols in the rounded style with fill, weight 400, grade 0 and optical size 24.
Match the icon size to the text next to it.
Prefer familiar, learned symbols for an action or status.
Use a given icon for exactly one purpose across the interface.
donts: Don't use icons whose meaning is unclear or ambiguous.
Don't overload the interface with icons.
Don't reuse an established symbol, such as the magnifier for search, for a different function.

docs.summary: Icons are the small symbols that mark actions, content and status. KERN draws them from Google Material Symbols in the rounded, filled style with weight 400, grade 0 and optical size 24, in four sizes. Use them sparingly, only where they add value, and keep one icon to one meaning.

sections.heading: Kurzbeschreibung
sections.summary: Icons are small graphic symbols that show or emphasise actions, content or status.

sections.heading: Beschreibung
sections.summary: KERN uses Google Material Symbols in the rounded style with the fill option and the typographic settings weight 400, grade 0 and optical size 24. The result is balanced and soft, and each icon can be used in one of four sizes.

sections.heading: Verwendungsregeln
sections.summary: Icons must be clear and intuitive and are best supported by text. Use them sparingly and only where they add value, for example to mark an action or a status. Give each icon a single function and keep it consistent across the interface: the magnifier means search and should not also mean zoom.

sections.heading: Dos und Don’ts
sections.summary: Balance the icon size against the text beside it, avoid unclear icons, do not overload the interface with icons, prefer familiar symbols, and use one icon for one purpose only.

components.title: Input Date
components.summary: Input Date splits a date into day, month and year fields, grouped under one label that states the expected order.

whenToUse: Use Input Date when a form needs a date, such as a birth date or the expiry date of a document.
dos: Give the group a clear shared label and a hint that states the format.
Use examples such as 14 4 2014 so the day and month order is unambiguous.
Mirror the source document's format when the date is copied from a passport or a card.
Keep the three fields at their default size.
donts: Don't use disabled, because it restricts accessibility.
Don't require leading zeros.
Don't change the size of the day, month and year fields.

docs.summary: Input Date helps users enter a date. It splits the value into separate day, month and year fields, grouped and labelled as one unit with a hint that shows the order, for example 14 4 2014. Keep the field sizes as delivered, and choose examples that make the day and month order unambiguous.

sections.heading: Kurzbeschreibung
sections.summary: Input Date helps users enter a date.

sections.heading: Disabled
sections.summary: Avoid disabled, because it restricts accessibility.

sections.heading: Beschreibung
sections.summary: The general input properties apply. Three separate fields take day, month and year, grouped under one shared label, with a hint below giving the format, for example 14 4 2014. The fields read as one unit, and their size should stay unchanged so the layout stays stable.

sections.heading: Verwendungsregeln
sections.summary: Used in forms to enter a date; the design follows the kind of date, for example a birth date or an expiry date copied from a document, whose format the fields should mirror. Choose examples that make the day and month order obvious, like 14 4 2014. Leading zeros are not required.

sections.heading: Dos und Don’ts
sections.summary: The general Input Dos and Don'ts apply, plus keeping the day, month and year fields at their default size so the layout stays stable.

components.title: Input E-Mail
components.summary: Input E-Mail accepts one email address, validates its format and reports invalid entries below the field.

whenToUse: Use Input E-Mail wherever a form needs an email address, for example registration or contact details.
dos: Allow autocomplete so an address the user entered before can be completed.
Explain the expected format in the hint text.
donts: Don't use the field for anything other than email addresses.
Don't use disabled, because it restricts accessibility.

docs.summary: Input E-Mail takes a single email address and checks the format automatically, for example name@domain.tld, showing an error below the field when the entry is invalid. Use it only for email addresses, describe the expected format in the hint, and allow autocomplete so a previously typed address can be completed.

sections.heading: Kurzbeschreibung
sections.summary: Input E-Mail helps users enter an email address.

sections.heading: Disabled
sections.summary: Avoid disabled, since it restricts accessibility.

sections.heading: Beschreibung
sections.summary: The general input properties apply. The field takes an email address and automatically checks that it follows the basic structure, for example username@domain.tld, and shows an error message for invalid input. It supports all the input states.

sections.heading: Verwendungsregeln
sections.summary: Use Input E-Mail only to enter email addresses, and give help with the expected format.

sections.heading: Dos und Don’ts
sections.summary: Allow the autocomplete function so the email address is completed when the user has entered it before.

sections.heading: Weitere Hinweise
sections.summary: Refers to the general Dos and Don'ts for Input.

components.title: Input File
components.summary: Input File uploads one or more files by drag and drop or a file picker, and requires allowed formats and a size limit.

whenToUse: Use Input File when users must provide something only they can, such as their own photo or a receipt.
dos: Always state the allowed file types and the maximum size precisely.
Keep the label short and specific about what should be uploaded.
Validate uploads automatically and describe errors so users can fix them.
Allow a range of file formats.
donts: Don't ask for an upload unless the service really needs it.
Don't request data an API or the user's profile can already supply.
Don't group unrelated files in one Input File.
Don't use disabled, because it restricts accessibility.

docs.summary: Input File lets users upload one or more files, either by dragging them onto the drop area or with a button that opens the file browser. One file appears next to the button with its name and extension; several are summarised, for example "4 files selected". State the allowed formats and the maximum size in the hint.

sections.heading: Kurzbeschreibung
sections.summary: Input File enables the upload of one or more files.

sections.heading: Disabled
sections.summary: Avoid disabled, because it restricts accessibility.

sections.heading: Beschreibung
sections.summary: Users drag files onto the drop area, which reacts while the pointer is over it, or open the file browser with a button. One file is shown by name and extension, several are summarised. Keep the label specific and put the allowed formats and the maximum size in the hint; read-only is not supported.

sections.heading: Verwendungsregeln
sections.summary: Ask for an upload only when the service needs it, and check whether an API or the user's profile can supply the information instead. If you must ask, it should be something only the user can provide, such as a photo or a receipt. Allow several formats, validate automatically and describe errors.

sections.heading: Dos und Don’ts
sections.summary: Always state the allowed file types and the maximum size precisely.

sections.heading: Weitere Hinweise
sections.summary: Files uploaded together should belong together thematically; otherwise use several Input File components. The general Input Dos and Don'ts also apply.

components.title: Input Group
components.summary: Input Group adds a visual prefix, suffix or action to one field; it is not part of the value and must be explained in the label.

whenToUse: Use Input Group when a fixed part of the value, a unit or a related action should sit directly on the field.
Use it for standardised entries, such as a URL prefix, where part of the value is already given.
dos: Write the label so the context is unambiguous, for example costs in euro.
Keep the label outside the input group.
Use universally understood prefixes and suffixes such as %.
Still process values that contain a manually typed prefix or suffix.
donts: Don't use an input group when the field is self-explanatory.
Don't use ambiguous abbreviations or long, complex prefix and suffix content.
Don't let prefixes and suffixes distract from the actual input.
Don't use disabled, because it restricts accessibility.

docs.summary: Input Group adds a prefix, suffix or action to a single field, for example a unit, a currency or a button. These parts are not part of the value and assistive technology does not read them, so the label or supporting text must carry their meaning. Focus and validation behave as for one input, with errors below the group.

sections.heading: Kurzbeschreibung
sections.summary: An Input Group extends a field with a prefix, a suffix or an action to make the expected value clearer or to process it directly.

sections.heading: Disabled
sections.summary: Avoid disabled, because it restricts accessibility.

sections.heading: Beschreibung
sections.summary: The general input properties apply. Text or interactive parts sit before or after the field and clarify the context; they are not part of the value. Focus and validation apply to the input, and errors appear below the group. The label must carry the meaning for assistive technology.

sections.heading: Verwendungsregeln
sections.summary: Use Input Groups deliberately and for the context in hand: for units such as euro, percent or kilogram, for URL prefixes, or for an action tied to the entry, such as showing and hiding a password. They suit standardised input where part of the value is fixed.

sections.heading: Dos und Don’ts
sections.summary: Write the label so the context is clear, for example costs in euro rather than just costs, and keep it outside the group. Still handle values with a manually typed prefix. Skip the group when the field is self-explanatory, prefer signs such as %, and use prefixes sparingly.

components.title: Input Number
components.summary: Input Number accepts a number through inputmode="numeric" and reports validation errors below the field.

whenToUse: Use Input Number for unpredictable numeric values such as a postcode, a house number or an area size.
dos: Make the label show that only numbers are expected, for example a house number or a postcode.
Explain the permitted characters in the hint when the label does not make it obvious.
Use inputmode="numeric" so users get a numeric keypad.
donts: Don't use Input Number when the answer options are known; use Select, Checkboxes or Radios.
Don't use it for a phone number or a date; Input Tel and Input Date fit better.
Don't use disabled, because it restricts accessibility.

docs.summary: Input Number takes a number. The field uses inputmode="numeric", so mobile users get a numeric keypad, and it validates the entry and shows errors below the field. The label should make clear that only digits belong here; otherwise the hint must list the characters that are allowed. The width can be adjusted.

sections.heading: Kurzbeschreibung
sections.summary: Input Number helps users enter a number.

sections.heading: Disabled
sections.summary: Avoid disabled, because it restricts accessibility.

sections.heading: Beschreibung
sections.summary: The general input properties apply. inputmode="numeric" gives users a numeric keypad, typically on mobile devices. Keep the label short and clear, optionally marked as optional, and use the hint for the format. Validation reports problems below the field, and the width can be adjusted.

sections.heading: Verwendungsregeln
sections.summary: Used where the expected number cannot be predicted. If the answer options are known, prefer Select, Checkboxes or Radios; for a phone number or a date use Input Tel or Input Date. The label must show that only numbers are allowed, otherwise the hint must list the permitted characters.

sections.heading: Dos und Don’ts
sections.summary: For other fixed number formats, such as phone numbers or dates, use Input Tel or Input Date; when the options are known, use Select, Checkboxes or Radios. The general Input Dos and Don'ts also apply.

components.title: Input Password
components.summary: Input Password masks the entry, adds a visibility toggle and keeps browser autofill for passwords off.

dos: Use autocomplete="current-password" or autocomplete="new-password".
Explain the password rules in the help during registration.
Return a neutral error message on a failed sign-in.
donts: Don't drop autocomplete without good reason; browsers expect it.
Don't reveal whether the user name or the password was wrong.
Don't use Input Password for other text input.

docs.summary: Input Password masks what users type and offers a visibility toggle so typos can be spotted. A forgot-password link sits below the field and should lead to a form for requesting a new password. Autofill is switched off in password fields for privacy, and all input states except disabled and read-only are supported.

sections.heading: Kurzbeschreibung
sections.summary: Input Password allows a password to be entered or created.

sections.heading: Beschreibung
sections.summary: The general input properties apply. Characters appear masked as dots, and an icon button to the right shows or hides them, helping avoid typos. A link below the field leads to a form for requesting a new password. Autofill is off for privacy; all states except disabled and read-only are supported.

sections.heading: Verwendungsregeln
sections.summary: Input Password is used during sign-in or registration to enter a password. Do not use it for other text input.

sections.heading: Dos und Don’ts
sections.summary: Explain the rules for creating a password during registration, and use autocomplete="current-password" or autocomplete="new-password". Do not drop autocomplete without good reason. On a failed sign-in, do not reveal whether the user name or the password was wrong.

components.title: Input Tel
components.summary: Input Tel takes a phone number with type="tel" and allows digits plus characters such as +.

whenToUse: Use Input Tel for phone numbers, such as a landline or mobile number, including international prefixes.
dos: Use type="tel" so mobile users get a numeric keypad.
Tell users the expected format in the hint text.
Make the label show that a phone number is expected, for example a mobile number.
donts: Don't use Input Tel for general numbers; Input Number fits better.
Don't use disabled, because it restricts accessibility.

docs.summary: Input Tel takes a phone number. The field uses type="tel", so mobile users get a numeric keypad, and it allows characters such as + for a country code. The label should state that a phone number is expected; if a particular format is required, the hint must explain the allowed characters. Validation errors appear below the field.

sections.heading: Kurzbeschreibung
sections.summary: Input Tel helps users enter a phone number.

sections.heading: Disabled
sections.summary: Avoid disabled, since it restricts accessibility.

sections.heading: Beschreibung
sections.summary: The general input properties apply. type="tel" gives mobile users a numeric keypad, and characters such as + for a country code are allowed. Keep the label clear about the expected value, optionally marked as optional, and use a hint for the format. Validation reports problems below the field.

sections.heading: Verwendungsregeln
sections.summary: Used in forms to enter a phone number; for general numbers Input Number fits better. The label should make clear that a phone number is expected, for example a mobile or landline number. If that is not obvious, the hint must explain the allowed characters and format.

sections.heading: Dos und Don’ts
sections.summary: Use Input Tel only for phone numbers; for numbers in general Input Number is the better choice. Point users to the expected format. The general Input Dos and Don'ts also apply.

components.title: Input Text
components.summary: Input Text is the basic single-line field for alphanumeric input whose value cannot be predicted.

whenToUse: Use Input Text for free-form, single-line entries such as a name, a street or a short note.
dos: Use Input Text for single-line entries whose value cannot be predicted.
Show the validation message below the field.
donts: Don't use free text when users choose from a known list; use Checkboxes or Radios.
Don't use Input Text for longer, multi-line input; use Text Area.
Don't use disabled, because it restricts accessibility.

docs.summary: Input Text is the basic single-line field for alphanumeric input: letters, digits and special characters. It supports validation and shows an error message below the field, and its width can be adjusted. Use it when the expected entry cannot be predicted, not when the options are known or when the text is multi-line.

sections.heading: Kurzbeschreibung
sections.summary: Input Text lets users enter letters, digits and special characters.

sections.heading: Disabled
sections.summary: Avoid disabled, because it restricts accessibility.

sections.heading: Beschreibung
sections.summary: The general input properties apply. A text field is a basic component that takes alphanumeric data, letters, digits and special characters, and can be adapted for different input types. Validation reports problems below the field, the width can be adjusted and all input states are supported.

sections.heading: Verwendungsregeln
sections.summary: Use Input Text when the expected entry is single-line and cannot be predicted. If the answer options are known and selectable, prefer Checkboxes or Radios, and for longer multi-line entries use Text Area.

sections.heading: Dos und Don’ts
sections.summary: When users choose from a predefined list, avoid free text: it is more error-prone and makes data harder to compare or match. Use Checkboxes or Radio buttons instead.

sections.heading: Weitere Hinweise
sections.summary: Refers to the general Dos and Don'ts for Input.

components.title: Input Url
components.summary: Input Url takes a web address in a type="url" field and validates its format.

whenToUse: Use Input Url when a form needs an internet address, for example the address of a service.
dos: Use the field only for internet addresses.
Point users to the expected format in the hint text.
Make the label show that a web address is expected.
donts: Don't use disabled, because it restricts accessibility.
Don't leave the accepted format unstated; the label or hint must give it.

docs.summary: Input Url takes a web address through a type="url" field and validates the format automatically. The label should make clear that only internet addresses belong here; if a particular format is expected, the hint must state the allowed characters. Errors appear below the field, and the width can be adjusted.

sections.heading: Kurzbeschreibung
sections.summary: Input Url helps users enter an internet address (URL).

sections.heading: Disabled
sections.summary: Avoid disabled, because it restricts accessibility.

sections.heading: Beschreibung
sections.summary: The general input properties apply. The field uses input type="url" for web addresses, allowing alphanumeric characters and the special characters a URL permits, and validates the format. Errors appear below the field, the width can be adjusted and all input states are supported.

sections.heading: Verwendungsregeln
sections.summary: Input Url is used in forms to enter an internet address. The label should make clear that only addresses may be entered; if that is not obvious, or a particular format is expected, the hint must explain the allowed characters and the format.

sections.heading: Dos and Don’ts
sections.summary: Use Input Url only for internet addresses, and point users to the expected format. The general Input Dos and Don'ts also apply.

components.title: Kopfzeile
components.summary: Kopfzeile is the fixed top banner that marks a public administration site; none of its parts may be changed.

whenToUse: Use it on authorities' sites, online services and service portals to identify an official government offer.
Use it to make an offer recognisable and trustworthy; using the umbrella brand elements is voluntary.
dos: Use the Kopfzeile only for digital presences of public bodies.
Place it at the very top and let it scroll with the content.
Align its content left with the main content area, usually done manually in code.
Leave size, colour, font, content and position exactly as delivered.
Use the container variant when the content should follow the page grid.
donts: Don't change any part of the banner: size, colour, font, content or position.
Don't place it between content blocks or at the bottom of the page.
Don't make the banner sticky.
Don't publish a custom design without agreement from the umbrella brand coordination group.

docs.summary: The Kopfzeile is one of the four elements of the digital umbrella brand and marks a website as an official public administration presence. It is a narrow coloured banner at the very top, with the German flag and the official wording beside it. Its parts are tested and must not be changed; it scrolls with the page and is never sticky.

sections.heading: Kurzbeschreibung
sections.summary: The Kopfzeile marks digital presences of public administration, such as authorities, online services and service portals.

sections.heading: Container Kopfzeile
sections.summary: Shows the markup for the container variant, where the bar spans the full browser width and the content aligns with the page container.

sections.heading: Fluid Kopfzeile
sections.summary: Shows the markup for the fluid variant, which has no side margin.

sections.heading: Webkomponente
sections.summary: Most KERN components are plain HTML and CSS for flexibility; the Kopfzeile is also shipped as a web component so it stays consistent and can be updated centrally instead of editing every page.

sections.heading: Via Script-Datei:
sections.summary: Shows how to load the web component from a script file or the CDN.

sections.heading: Oder via NPM-Paket:
sections.summary: Shows how to load the web component from the npm package.

sections.heading: Standard:
sections.summary: Shows the default markup of the Kopfzeile.

sections.heading: Mit eigenem Label (z. B. für Mandanten):
sections.summary: Shows the markup with a custom label, for example for a tenant.

sections.heading: Mit benutzerdefinierten Breakpoints:
sections.summary: Shows the markup with custom breakpoints.

sections.heading: Mit explizitem Theme:
sections.summary: Shows the markup with an explicitly set light or dark theme; by default the theme follows the user's system setting (prefers-color-scheme).

sections.heading: Inhalt (Children)
sections.summary: The content between the tags can be a custom label; the default is the standard official wording.

sections.heading: Beschreibung
sections.summary: One of four elements of the digital umbrella brand, used voluntarily. The narrow top banner is a trust anchor: the German flag with the official wording to its right, on a full-width coloured background. The container variant aligns content left with the page grid, at most 1536 pixels wide.

sections.heading: Verwendungsregeln
sections.summary: Used on digital presences of authorities, online services and service portals; the placement at the very top lets users identify an official government offer immediately.

sections.heading: Nutzen der Kopfzeile
sections.summary: Three benefits: quick recognition, simple and inexpensive implementation, and a trust anchor.

sections.heading: Beispiele
sections.summary: Lists examples: Service Justiz, GOVDATA, the national feedback component and the Bundesportal.

sections.heading: Dos and Don’ts
sections.summary: Only public bodies may use it, aligned left with the main content area, usually done manually in code. Nothing may change in size, colour, font, content or position, and it belongs at the very top, never between content blocks or at the bottom. It scrolls with the content and is never sticky.

components.title: Label
components.summary: Label is the short text that names an input, button or control; it sits above the element.

whenToUse: Use Label for inputs, selects, checkboxes, radios and buttons that need a name.
Use label-large for particularly prominent input areas or complex form structures.
Use label-subtle when a label should recede within the information hierarchy.
dos: Write labels clearly and precisely, for example an email address rather than a generic input.
Give every interactive element a label.
Place the label above its element by default; inside works only for compact variants.
Keep labels short enough to read on one line.
Use the provided sizes and the subtle variant instead of custom styling.
donts: Don't restyle labels by hand; use the provided variants.
Don't use a label for explanatory text or longer hints; use Body instead.

docs.summary: Label is the short text that names an interactive element so users can tell what it does. It sits above its element, or to the right of a checkbox or radio, and comes in three sizes plus a subtle variant with a lighter weight. Keep it to a few clear words, style it only through the provided variants, and use Body for explanations.

sections.heading: Kurzbeschreibung
sections.summary: A Label names interactive elements and makes their function clear.

sections.heading: Beschreibung
sections.summary: A text component that names interactive elements so users can match fields, buttons and controls unambiguously. Keep it short and clear, placed above the element or, for checkboxes and radios, to its right. Sizes small, default and large exist, plus a subtle variant with a reduced type weight.

sections.heading: Verwendungsregeln
sections.summary: Use label-default for inputs, selects and controls such as Select, Checkbox and Radio, or buttons. label-large suits prominent input areas or complex forms, label-small fits tight space so use it sparingly, and label-subtle lets labels recede while staying readable and clearly assigned.

sections.heading: Dos und Don’ts
sections.summary: Write labels clearly and precisely, for example an email address rather than a generic input. Label every interactive element, place it above by default and keep it short enough for one line. Use the provided variants instead of custom styles, and use Body for explanatory text or longer hints.

components.title: Layers
Link
components.summary: A Link navigates to other content; mark different targets with icons and never use it to change data.

whenToUse: Use a Link to navigate to another page, section, document or email address.
Use the kern-btn class when a link should look like a button for navigation that changes no data.
Use the small variant where a link should carry less visual weight, not for primary navigation.
dos: Distinguish internal, external, email and download targets with different icons.
Give different targets on one page distinct link texts instead of one generic phrase.
Add a second cue besides colour, such as an underline or an icon.
Always give a link visible text, even when an icon is present.
Keep link text short but precise.
donts: Don't use a link as a button for an action that changes data, for example in forms.
Don't use the linked URL as the link text.
Don't use an icon on its own without text.
Don't overload the page with links.
Don't remove the visited state except in exceptional cases.

docs.summary: A Link is a direct connection to other content. It is set apart from body text by colour and changes colour once visited, and different targets are marked with icons: internal, back, download, external, email, sign language and easy language. Links inside running text carry no icon; outside text an icon helps highlight the target. Use text, never an icon alone.

sections.heading: Kurzbeschreibung
sections.summary: A Link is a direct connection to other content.

sections.heading: Link als Button darstellen
sections.summary: The class kern-btn makes a link look like a button. This can help in forms or processes when navigating to another page or section is needed without changing data.

sections.heading: Link ohne besuchten Zustand
sections.summary: The class kern-link--no-visited-state turns off the default visited state. Because that can make orientation harder, use it only in exceptional cases.

sections.heading: Beschreibung
sections.summary: A link is an interactive element made of text, or an icon plus text, set apart from other text by colour. Once clicked it changes colour, so users can see which links they already followed. Inside running text links carry no icon; outside text an icon highlights the target.

sections.heading: Verwendungsregeln
sections.summary: The icons mark the target: an arrow right for internal links, an arrow left for going back, a download arrow for documents, open-in-new for external pages, an envelope for email, plus symbols for sign language and easy-language content.

sections.heading: Link small
sections.summary: The small variant suits areas where the link should carry less visual weight. Do not use it for primary navigation; the default Link is the better choice there.

sections.heading: Dos und Don’ts
sections.summary: Distinguish internal, external, email and download targets with different icons, and give different targets distinct link texts instead of one generic phrase. Add a second cue besides colour to text links, such as an underline or icon, and never use a link to change data or the URL as its text.

sections.heading: Weitere Hinweise
sections.summary: Keep link text short but precise, and do not overload a page with links.

components.title: List
components.summary: List groups related items as a bulleted, numbered or plain list, in three sizes or a horizontal layout.

docs.summary: List structures related content into ordered, unordered or description lists, which makes the content easier to scan and compare. It offers the marker styles none, bullet and number, three sizes, and a horizontal layout. The usage rules and Dos and Don'ts for the component are not published yet.

sections.heading: Kurzbeschreibung
sections.summary: Lists structure related content into ordered, unordered or description lists for better readability and clarity.

sections.heading: Beschreibung
sections.summary: Lists are a fundamental element for structuring content; they present related information clearly and improve readability.

sections.heading: Verwendungsregeln
sections.summary: The usage rules for List are not published in the documentation yet; the section is a placeholder.

sections.heading: Do's and Don'ts
sections.summary: The Dos and Don'ts for List are not published in the documentation yet; the section is a placeholder.

components.title: Loader
components.summary: Animated spinner that signals an ongoing load; use it when the expected wait is not known but likely exceeds one second.

whenToUse: Signalling an unknown wait that is expected to last longer than about one second.
Fetching or refreshing search results, signing in, downloads, or loading large content such as videos.
dos: Use a loader when the expected wait is not exactly known but is likely to take more than one second.
donts: Do not show a loading indicator when the expected wait is less than one second.
Do not use several loaders at the same time.

docs.summary: Loader is an animated spinning icon that tells users content is loading. It signals that a request is being processed and is used when the expected wait is unknown but likely longer than one second. A transparent white background (colour and transparency tokens in Figma) sits behind it so the loader stays clearly visible. Typical cases are fetching or refreshing search results, signing in to protected areas, downloads and loading large content such as videos.

sections.heading: Kurzbeschreibung
sections.summary: An animated, spinning icon that tells users that content is loading.

sections.heading: Beschreibung
sections.summary: Indicates that a loading or computation process is running. The icon animates continuously to signal to users that their request is being processed.

sections.heading: Verwendungsregeln
sections.summary: Use a loader when the expected wait is not exactly known but is likely to exceed one second. The component sits on a transparent white background (colour and transparency tokens in Figma) so it stays clearly visible.

sections.heading: Beispiele
sections.summary: Typical cases: fetching new or refreshed search results, signing in to protected areas, downloading content, and loading large content such as videos.

sections.heading: Dos und Don’ts
sections.summary: Do not show a loading indicator when the wait is less than one second, and never use several loaders at the same time.
