components.title: Preline
components.summary: Adds short supporting text above a Title or Heading; never used standalone.

whenToUse: To mark a topic area, category or introduction above a title.
dos: Keep the Preline text short and to the point, for example a context hint or a category label.
donts: Do not use Preline as a standalone heading; it always supplements a Title or Heading.
Do not use Preline for long explanations or running text; use the Body component for that.
Do not use Preline without a clear link to the heading it belongs to.
Do not add bold, italic or other text formatting; the style already provides it.
Do not combine Preline with a size that differs from the heading or title it accompanies.
Do not use Preline to structure the page; the Heading component is solely responsible for that.

docs.summary: Preline adds short supporting information to a Title or Heading. It is a text component that gives the heading below it more context while staying visually and hierarchically in the background, and it is never used on its own. It comes in three sizes: large, default and small. Match the size to the heading or title below it and place the Preline directly above that heading with no extra spacing, since the vertical rhythm is already in the styles.

sections.heading: Kurzbeschreibung
sections.summary: Adds explanatory information to a Title or Heading.

sections.heading: Beschreibung
sections.summary: Usually a short explanatory text that deepens the context of the Heading or Title below it. It sits above that heading, stays visually and hierarchically in the background, and comes in three sizes: large, default and small.

sections.heading: Verwendungsregeln
sections.summary: Use Preline to mark a topic area, category or introduction above a title. It is never standalone and always pairs with the Title or Heading below it; match its size to that heading and place it directly above with no extra spacing, since the styles already handle the vertical rhythm.

sections.heading: Dos und Don’ts
sections.summary: Keep the text short and to the point, for example a context hint or a category. Do not use Preline as a standalone heading, for longer explanations or body copy, without a clear link to the heading that follows, with extra bold or italic styling, with inconsistent sizes, or to structure the page.

components.title: Progress
components.summary: Shows progress through a multi-step process; use it for fixed-order flows, not for loading.

whenToUse: Processes with a fixed sequence of steps, such as registration or payment flows.
To break a complex process into smaller, easier-to-follow steps.
dos: Use Progress for linear, chronological processes that need a fixed step order.
donts: Do not use Progress for loading processes.
Avoid Progress for very long or complex processes with more than ten steps; it can overwhelm users.

docs.summary: Progress shows the overall duration and progress of a multi-step process and gives continuous feedback on which step users are in and how many remain. It splits a longer process into equal segments; if extra steps become necessary the remaining segments can be re-divided. Users move linearly, or non-linearly where allowed, and the component is not interactive. A label is optional but recommended; it can sit above or below the bar and should name the active step and the total.

sections.heading: Kurzbeschreibung
sections.summary: Shows the overall duration and progress of a multi-step process.

sections.heading: Beschreibung
sections.summary: Gives continuous feedback on the current step and how many remain. The bar is split into equal steps and can be re-divided if the process grows. Users move linearly or non-linearly; the component is not interactive. A label is optional but recommended and names the active step and total.

sections.heading: Verwendungsregeln
sections.summary: Suited to processes that run in a fixed order, breaking a complex process into smaller, easier steps. Typical cases are steps in an online service, a registration process or a payment process.

sections.heading: Dos und Don’ts
sections.summary: Do not use Progress for loading processes; use a Loader for those.

sections.heading: Weitere Hinweise
sections.summary: Use Progress for linear, chronological processes that require a fixed order of steps. Avoid it for very long or complex processes with more than ten steps, which can overwhelm users.

components.title: Input Radios
components.summary: Lets users select exactly one option from a mutually exclusive group.

whenToUse: Forms where users must choose exactly one of several mutually exclusive options.
dos: Write each radio label as a statement rather than a question where possible.
Keep radio labels short so they can be grasped quickly.
Phrase radio labels positively where possible, avoiding '... not ...' or '... no ...'.
Preselect an option only for settings; when the choice answers a question, leave all options unselected.
donts: Never allow more than one option of a radio group to be selected.
Do not use the readonly state; radios accept all other Input states.

docs.summary: Radios let users pick exactly one option from a set of mutually exclusive options. A radio group always has a label making clear what the choice refers to, and it can be marked optional; each radio is labelled as briefly as possible. A hint can add detail, help can be offered for longer explanations, and error messages are shown below the group. All Input states apply except readonly. Two options sit horizontally, more stack vertically. Preselect only for settings, not for a question.

sections.heading: Kurzbeschreibung
sections.summary: Let users pick only one option from mutually exclusive options.

sections.heading: Beschreibung
sections.summary: A radio group lets users choose which option applies, always one and never several. The group always has a label, individual radios are labelled as briefly as possible, a hint or help can add detail, error messages appear below the group, and all Input states apply except readonly.

sections.heading: Verwendungsregeln
sections.summary: Use radios in forms when users must choose one of several options, for example how they want to identify themselves. Two radios are shown horizontally; more than two stack vertically. Preselect an option only for settings; when the choice answers a question, none should be selected up front.

sections.heading: Dos und Don’ts
sections.summary: Never allow more than one option of a radio group to be selected. Write a radio label as a statement rather than a question where possible, and keep it short so it is easy to take in.

sections.heading: Weitere Hinweise
sections.summary: Phrase a radio label positively where possible, avoiding constructions such as '... not ...' or '... no ...'.

components.title: Search
components.summary: Search field plus button, built on Input Group, for finding content with a search term.

whenToUse: When users should search content, documents or data, such as administrative services.
For dynamic, iterative lookups where users try and refine several search terms.
dos: Place the search in the same position on every page.
Make sure the search term can be reset via a clear function or the browser's native behaviour.
Keep the search term in the field after submitting so users can refine it.
Use the variant without a visible label only in justified exceptions, such as the header.
If the search button shows only an icon, always provide a label for accessibility.
donts: Do not use placeholder text instead of a visible label; placeholders disappear while typing.
Do not reduce search to a magnifier icon on desktop when it is relevant to task success.
Do not hide a central search behind several steps on mobile devices.

docs.summary: Search lets users find content and information quickly with a search term. It combines a search field and a search button and is built on the Input Group; some browsers add a native clear function. It comes in standard and block variants, several sizes and different button styles. Search is dynamic and iterative: users try several terms and refine them. Keep it in the same place throughout, with a global search expected top right, and never use a placeholder instead of a visible label.

sections.heading: Kurzbeschreibung
sections.summary: Lets users find content and information, such as administrative services, quickly with a search term.

sections.heading: Search mit Label und Icon-Only Button
sections.summary: If the search button uses only an icon, a label is mandatory for accessibility reasons.

sections.heading: Search ohne Label
sections.summary: Use a search without a visible label only in justified exceptions, such as in the header. Otherwise the search needs a visible label, and without one its purpose must be named programmatically, for example via aria-label.

sections.heading: Beschreibung
sections.summary: Search consists of a search field and a search button and is based on the Input Group, combining an input with an action that triggers the search. Some browsers add a native clear function. The component comes as a standard or block variant, with several sizes and different button styles.

sections.heading: Verwendungsregeln
sections.summary: Use Search when users should target content or data. Unlike classic form input, it is dynamic and iterative, so keep its position consistent. Never use a placeholder instead of a visible label, and make the button primary only when search is the key action on the page.

sections.heading: Dos und Don'ts
sections.summary: Place search consistently, make the term easy to reset, and keep the term in the field after submitting so users can refine it. Do not use placeholder text instead of a visible label, reduce search to a magnifier icon on desktop, or hide central search behind several steps on mobile.

components.title: Input Select
components.summary: Single-choice drop-down list; use it for 5 to 15 options and favour radios where possible.

whenToUse: Forms where users pick exactly one of 5 to 15 predefined options.
When space is tight or input errors must be avoided.
dos: Keep the labels of the values in the list as short as possible.
donts: Avoid the disabled state, because it limits accessibility.
Do not use a select as a way to trigger actions or as navigation.
Do not use more than 15 values in the selection list; the right option becomes hard to find.

docs.summary: Select lets users choose one option from a drop-down list. Users open the list by clicking or focusing with the keyboard; the current value is highlighted in the open list and shown on the closed element, and text cannot be typed directly. The label should be short and precise, and a hint can explain the options. Errors appear below the field and the width can be adapted. All Input states apply except readonly. Use it for 5 to 15 options, never to trigger actions or as navigation.

sections.heading: Kurzbeschreibung
sections.summary: Lets users choose one option from a drop-down list of options.

sections.heading: Disabled
sections.summary: Avoid the disabled state, because it limits accessibility.

sections.heading: Beschreibung
sections.summary: Select allows exactly one option from a predefined list, opened by click or keyboard focus. The current value is highlighted in the open list and shown when closed, and free text cannot be entered. Errors appear below the field, and all Input states apply except readonly.

sections.heading: Verwendungsregeln
sections.summary: Use a select to choose options in forms, not to reach actions or as navigation, with 5 to 15 options and one selectable value. Selects are hard to use, so prefer asking for information with Input Radios or Input Checkboxes; keep a select for tight space or to avoid input errors.

sections.heading: Dos und Don’ts
sections.summary: Keep the labels of the values in the list as short as possible.

sections.heading: Weitere Hinweise
sections.summary: Use at most 15 values in the list; more makes it hard to find the right option, so prefer radios where possible. Preselect a value only for a setting that is already active, otherwise the preselection can sway users or hide the need to choose.

components.title: Subline
components.summary: Adds short supporting text below a Title or Heading; never used standalone.

whenToUse: To add supporting context below a Title or Heading.
dos: Keep the Subline text short and to the point, for example a context hint or a category label.
donts: Do not use Subline as a standalone heading; it always supplements a Title or Heading.
Do not use Subline for long explanations or running text; use the Body component.
Do not use Subline without a clear link to the statement above it.
Do not add bold, italic or other text formatting; the style already provides it.
Do not combine Subline with a size that differs from the heading or title above it.
Do not use Subline to structure the page; the Heading component is solely responsible for that.

docs.summary: Subline adds short supporting information below a Title or Heading. It is a text component that gives the heading above it more context while staying visually and hierarchically in the background, and it is never used on its own. It comes in three sizes: large, default and small. Match the size to the heading or title above it and place the Subline directly below that heading with no extra spacing, since the vertical rhythm is already in the styles.

sections.heading: Kurzbeschreibung
sections.summary: Adds explanatory information below a Title or Heading.

sections.heading: Beschreibung
sections.summary: Usually a short explanatory text that deepens the context of the Heading or Title above it. It sits directly below that heading, stays visually and hierarchically in the background, and comes in three sizes: large, default and small.

sections.heading: Verwendungsregeln
sections.summary: Subline complements a Title or Heading visually and in content with extra information. It is never standalone and pairs closely with the heading above it; match its size to that heading and place it directly below with no extra spacing, since the styles already handle the vertical rhythm.

sections.heading: Dos und Don’ts
sections.summary: Keep the text short and to the point, for example a context hint or a category. Do not use Subline as a standalone heading, for longer explanations or body copy, without a clear link to the statement above it, with extra bold or italic styling, with inconsistent sizes, or to structure the page.

components.title: Summary
components.summary: Shows earlier form entries as term and value pairs so users can review and edit them.

whenToUse: After users entered information through a Task List or Task List group and need to review it before continuing.
Before sending a form, so entries can be checked calmly.
dos: Use the same wording for the same tasks and groups as in the related Task List or Task List group.
Show the information in the same order in which it was entered.
donts: Do not hide essential information; users must be able to see where to change their entries.
Do not use other buttons or actions inside the Summary.

docs.summary: Summary collects the information users entered in earlier forms and lets them edit it. It consists of a heading, a Description List and a link to edit, and several summaries form a summary group. The heading describes the preceding task, optionally numbered. Each Description List entry pairs the information asked for with the user's entry. Use it after users entered information via a Task List or Task List group, so they can review everything before continuing.

sections.heading: Kurzbeschreibung
sections.summary: Collects all information users entered in earlier forms, which they can edit if needed.

sections.heading: Beschreibung
sections.summary: A Summary has a heading, a Description List and a link to edit; several summaries form a summary group. The heading describes the preceding task, optionally with a number. Each Description List entry pairs the term (the information asked for) with the description (what the user entered).

sections.heading: Verwendungsregeln
sections.summary: Use Summary or a summary group when users entered information via a Task List or Task List group, so they can review all entries before continuing; it is only complete once every entry is made. Showing part of the information is fine to avoid overload, but only when users need not check everything.

sections.heading: Dos und Don’ts
sections.summary: Use the same wording as the related Task List or Task List group for the same tasks and groups. Do not hide essential information, so users know where to change entries, show the information in the order it was entered, and do not add other buttons or actions inside the Summary.

components.title: Table
components.summary: Presents structured data in rows and columns; static, with an optional action column.

whenToUse: For structured data that can be arranged meaningfully in rows and columns.
dos: Right-align values in columns that contain only numbers to make comparison easier.
Use visual emphasis such as bold for important data points.
Always use button size x-small for interaction elements in the action column.
Give action-column buttons a meaningful accessible name, linking them to the row header via aria-describedby when labels repeat or are icon-only.
donts: Do not use tables for unstructured content.
Do not use tables to lay out page content; use the Grid instead.
Do not overload a table with too many columns or too much data.
Do not use unexplained abbreviations or symbols.
Do not use Primary buttons inside a table; only Secondary and Tertiary are allowed.

docs.summary: Table presents structured data in rows and columns for easy comparison and quick scanning. It comes in two sizes, default and small. A table can have an action column at the right edge with right-aligned buttons; those always use button size x-small and only the Secondary and Tertiary variants, never Primary, so the page hierarchy stays intact. Action-column buttons need a meaningful accessible name; when labels repeat or are icon-only, link them to the row header via aria-describedby.

sections.heading: Kurzbeschreibung
sections.summary: Presents data in tabular form for easy comparison and quick scanning of information.

sections.heading: Aktionen
sections.summary: Tables can have an action column at the right edge, with the buttons inside its cells aligned to the right.

sections.heading: Buttons in Tabellen
sections.summary: Action-column interaction elements always use button size x-small. Only Secondary and Tertiary are allowed, never Primary. Buttons need an accessible name, linked to the row header via aria-describedby when labels repeat or are icon-only.

sections.heading: Beschreibung
sections.summary: A table is a static, tabular structure with one or more rows and several columns; it is not interactive. Rows can be striped for readability. The component comes in two sizes: default and small.

sections.heading: Bestandteile einer Tabelle:
sections.summary: Parts of a table: an optional Caption describing the content; the Head with column headings; the Body with the data rows, one record per row and one attribute per column; and an optional Footer below the body for totals or extra information.

sections.heading: Verwendungsregeln
sections.summary: Use the table for structured data that fits in rows and columns, with clear column headings and content ordered for quick scanning; with very many columns, consider another presentation. Right-align numbers, left-align text, align dates by convention. Check small screens for horizontal scrolling.

sections.heading: Dos
sections.summary: Do not use tables for unstructured content or to lay out a page; use the Grid for layout. Use visual emphasis such as bold for important data points, right-align values in numeric columns, do not overload the table with too many columns, and avoid unexplained abbreviations.

components.title: Tabs
components.summary: Lets users show content elements in a structured way and switch between them.

docs.summary: Tabs let users show content elements in a structured way and switch between them.

components.title: Task List
components.summary: Lists tasks with their completion status for longer, multi-step processes.

whenToUse: Longer processes spread over several steps, such as online services.
When the required information does not fit on one page or several sessions are needed.
When tasks can be completed in any order.
dos: Keep a Task List to at most 7 tasks.
Keep the number of groups in a Task List group manageable.
Write group and task labels short and clear so screen reader users can operate the list.
Communicate only the correct status of a task.
Number tasks across the whole list instead of restarting numbering per group.
donts: Do not invent additional statuses beyond the ones defined.
Do not add other buttons or actions inside the Task List.

docs.summary: Task List shows the tasks users must complete and marks each one's status. It has a heading and one or more Task List elements; a group of at least two lists is often useful, especially when a summary follows. Each element describes a task, links to its form and can carry numbering and status: new, incomplete, done or not yet editable.

sections.heading: Kurzbeschreibung
sections.summary: Shows all tasks users must complete and marks the status of each task.

sections.heading: Beschreibung
sections.summary: A Task List has a heading and one or more Task List elements; a group of at least two lists is often useful, especially when a summary follows. Each element describes a task, links to its form and can carry numbering and status: new, incomplete, done or not yet editable.

sections.heading: Verwendungsregeln
sections.summary: Use a Task List or group for longer processes such as online services, where users work through tasks over several steps, placed on its own page that is easy to reach. It suits information too extensive for one page, processes needing several sessions, and tasks in any order.

sections.heading: Dos und Don’ts
sections.summary: Keep to at most 7 tasks per Task List and keep the number of groups manageable. Write group and task labels short and clear for screen reader users. Communicate only the correct status, do not add other actions inside the Task List, and number tasks across the whole list.

components.title: Input Textarea
components.summary: Multi-line text input; use it only for paragraphs, otherwise use Input Text.

whenToUse: When users must enter multi-line text or paragraphs.
dos: Allow the copy and paste function.
Let users enlarge the field when long text entries are expected.
donts: Avoid the disabled state, because it limits accessibility.

docs.summary: Textarea lets users enter long, multi-line text. Its height can be set freely but is always greater than a single-line field, and its width can be adapted; users can resize it by dragging the bottom-right corner, and a vertical scrollbar appears once the content exceeds the height. The label should be short and precise, and a hint can explain format, meaning or background. Errors appear below the field, and all Input states apply.

sections.heading: Kurzbeschreibung
sections.summary: Lets users enter long text content.

sections.heading: Disabled
sections.summary: Avoid the disabled state, because it limits accessibility.

sections.heading: Beschreibung
sections.summary: A field for multi-line text. Its height can be set freely but is always larger than a single-line input. Users can resize it by dragging the bottom-right corner, and a scrollbar appears when the text outgrows the height. Errors appear below the field.

sections.heading: Verwendungsregeln
sections.summary: Use Textarea only when users must enter multi-line text or paragraphs; otherwise use Input Text, and set the height in proportion to the expected text. Open questions are often hard, so check whether a complex question can be split into simple answers, such as radios.

sections.heading: Dos und Don’ts
sections.summary: Allow copy and paste, and let users enlarge the field when long text entries are expected. See also the general Dos and Don'ts for Input.

components.title: Title
components.summary: Heading for components such as Cards, Dialogs or form sections; needs a matching HTML heading level.

whenToUse: To name a section inside a component clearly, such as in Dialogs, form groups or Cards.
dos: Mark up a Title with a matching HTML heading level so the visual structure is also semantic.
Choose the size (large, default, small) by available space and visual hierarchy.
donts: Do not add extra formatting such as bold inside a Title; the style already highlights it.
Do not use Title for longer texts or explanatory content; use the Body component.
Do not rely on Title alone to convey a section's function; add semantic structure for accessible use.

docs.summary: Title is used for headings inside components, such as Cards, Dialogs or form sections, in three sizes: small, default and large. It gives visual structure inside UI elements and helps users orient themselves quickly; it usually holds a short, concise text placed above the content it refers to. Visual structure is also content structure, so a Title must be marked up with a matching HTML heading element, as WCAG and BITV require.

sections.heading: Kurzbeschreibung
sections.summary: Used for headings inside components.

sections.heading: Beschreibung
sections.summary: Suited to headings inside components such as Cards, Dialogs or form sections, and available in three sizes: small, default and large. It provides visual structure inside UI elements and helps users orient themselves, usually holding a short, concise text placed above the content it refers to.

sections.heading: Verwendungsregeln
sections.summary: Use Title to name components concisely, such as Dialogs, form groups or Cards. Mark it up with a matching HTML heading element, as WCAG and BITV require. Use large for prominent titles, default for form sections and small for compact layouts.

sections.heading: Dos und Don’ts
sections.summary: Use Title to name a section inside a component clearly, and pick the size by available space and visual hierarchy. Do not add extra formatting such as bold, do not use Title for longer explanations, and do not make it the only cue for a section's function.
